subject: Food Science
title: Clarence Birdseye and Freezing
description: A 60-second lesson on Clarence Birdseye and Freezing.

hook.text: In 1912, fur trader Clarence Birdseye watched Inuit flash-freeze fish in Arctic wind at -40°C. The fish tasted fresh months later.

buildup.text: Slow freezing creates large ice crystals that rupture cell walls—making food mushy when thawed.

discovery.text: Birdseye invented the double-belt freezer in 1924—pressing packages between refrigerated metal plates.

twist.text: Clarence Birdseye and Freezing has a twist: the obvious interpretation usually breaks down.

climax.text: Birdseye sold his company and 168 patents to General Foods in 1929 for $22 million—over $380 million today.

punchline.text: An Arctic fur trader saw flash-freezing in nature, then built a billion-dollar industry.

quiz.question: Why is flash-freezing superior to slow freezing for food quality?
options: Rapid freezing creates tiny ice crystals that don't rupture cell walls—preserving texture
